questions.stem: The human heart has how many chambers?
questions.explanation: The human heart has four chambers — two upper atria and two lower ventricles — which keep oxygenated and deoxygenated blood fully separated. Fish have a 2-chambered heart; amphibians and most reptiles have a 3-chambered heart (crocodilians have 4). Mammals and birds have 4 chambers, a more efficient design for warm-blooded metabolism.

questions.stem: Which blood vessel carries oxygenated blood from the lungs to the heart?
questions.explanation: Pulmonary veins (four in humans) carry oxygenated blood from the lungs to the left atrium of the heart — the only veins to carry oxygenated blood. Pulmonary arteries carry deoxygenated blood from the right ventricle to the lungs — the only arteries to carry deoxygenated blood. The aorta is the largest artery (from the left ventricle); the vena cavae are the largest veins (to the right atrium).

questions.stem: The exchange of oxygen and carbon dioxide between the air and blood takes place in the:
questions.explanation: Alveoli — tiny thin-walled air-sacs at the ends of the bronchioles — are where gas exchange happens across a one-cell-thick membrane. Each human lung has ~300-500 million alveoli; the total surface area is about 70 m², roughly the size of a tennis court. The trachea (windpipe), bronchi and bronchioles are air-conducting tubes; the larynx (voice-box) sits above the trachea.

questions.stem: Digestion of starch begins in the human digestive system in the:
questions.explanation: Saliva contains the enzyme amylase (ptyalin), which starts breaking down starch into maltose in the mouth. Acidic stomach juice stops amylase; protein digestion starts in the stomach (pepsin + HCl). Final digestion and absorption of most nutrients — including remaining starch and the proteins — happens in the small intestine with pancreatic and intestinal enzymes. The large intestine mainly absorbs water and forms faeces.

questions.stem: The functional unit of the kidney, responsible for filtering blood and forming urine, is the:
questions.explanation: Each human kidney has about 1 million nephrons. A nephron consists of a glomerulus (ball of capillaries inside the Bowman's capsule) for filtration, followed by a tubule that reabsorbs useful substances (glucose, salts, water) back into blood. Neurons are the cells of the nervous system; alveoli are in the lungs; hepatocytes are liver cells.

questions.stem: The largest gland in the human body is the:
questions.explanation: The liver — about 1.5 kg in an adult — is the largest gland (and internal organ) in the body. Key functions: secretes bile to help fat digestion, stores glucose as glycogen, detoxifies drugs and metabolises alcohol, synthesises plasma proteins. The pancreas is both an endocrine (insulin, glucagon) and exocrine (digestive enzymes) gland. The thyroid and adrenals are small endocrine glands.

questions.stem: The cell in the human body that transmits nerve impulses is called a:
questions.explanation: A neuron has a cell body, dendrites (receive signals) and a long axon (transmits the signal). Impulses are carried as electrical spikes called action potentials and jump across synapses via chemical neurotransmitters. Nephrons are kidney cells; myocytes are muscle cells; osteocytes are bone cells. Humans have about 86 billion neurons in the brain.
